note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Start with real Texas growing habit in panels 6 (Jim Conrad, Uvalde) and 11 (Don Bosan-Bruno, Austin). Panel 10 shows Cody Stricker's Cotulla flowering culm and its genuine slender stem carrying several short radiating terminal racemes; panel 9 is Tyler Cannon's close Austin view of dense one-sided spikelet rows. Older panels 4 and 1 show mature dried stage. Radiating heads alone are not species proof: the separate DENSE LEFT culm in panel 0 is not assigned to this species; only the right-hand one-sided head gets source-backed arrows. To confirm hooded windmillgrass against C. verticillata and hybrid look-alikes, observe the mature inflated UPPER STERILE lemma at about 1 mm scale.
tiles.short: Recognize short crowded one-sided windmill racemes; confirm a swollen upper sterile hood for final ID
tiles.status: SOURCE-LABELLED TX FLOWERING CULM / SHORT ONE-SIDED RACEMES / LIVING BASE PHOTOGRAPHED; STERILE HOOD UNDISSECTED

tiles.heading: 02 · CROWN AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Use genuine target plants in panels 6 (Uvalde roadside), 11 (Austin narrow upright basal foliage), and 10 (Cotulla true slender attached flowering stem). These show growing tuft context, but the underground connected fibrous roots and any runners are HIDDEN, and nearby grasses in mixed vegetation may be other species. Texas A&M says short stolons sometimes occur, whereas NRCS also mentions short rhizomes; neither can be inferred here. The true ciliate MEMBRANOUS ligule is an INSIDE blade/sheath junction structure; no current photo opens it face-on beside a ruler. Do not mark an outer sheath edge, stem node or leaf hairs as that free membrane.
tiles.short: Living ground-level tufts photographed twice; connected roots and true inner 1-mm ligule not yet shown
tiles.status: TWO REAL IN-GROUND HABIT PHOTOS PRESENT; EXPOSED ROOTS, ANY RUNNERS AND TRUE MEASURED INNER LIGULE MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN ONE TINY SPIKELET
tiles.details: USDA's species-identified public-domain macro (panel 2) actually shows six WHOLE spikelet units and their rounded upper profiles beside a photographed 2-mm scale. They are not bare seeds. But the separately lifted upper sterile lemma is NOT yet individually proven. Jim Conrad's intact spikelets (panel 3) show marginal cilia, and his ripe raceme (panel 5) shows dark fruits. Mature spikelets are roughly 1.5–2 mm long, containing a lower fertile and small upper sterile floret; photograph one opened with 0.5-mm calibration. New panel 9 (Tyler Cannon) now shows actual Texas maturity-stage one-sided spikelet rows at closer range; it does not open the fertile vs sterile floret pair, isolate the glumes, or reveal the swollen upper sterile hood margin.
tiles.short: About 1.5–2 mm body; one fertile + one sterile floret
tiles.status: USDA TWO-MM WHOLE SPIKELETS PLUS ACTUAL AUSTIN ONE-SIDED ROWS; UPPER STERILE LEMMA STILL NOT ISOLATED

tiles.heading: 04 · KEEP GLUMES SEPARATE
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase reports a lower glume about 0.5–0.7 mm; Go Botany reports an upper glume around 1–1.5 mm, while Kew's prose also gives 0.5–0.7 mm for the upper glume and inconsistent ratios. Preserve this disagreement: measure BOTH glumes separately on a vouchered mature specimen with 0.5-mm calibration. Neither glume is the hood or the source of a long lemma awn.
tiles.short: Two basal glumes; upper-glume sources disagree
tiles.status: SOURCE GLUME DIMENSION CONFLICT RETAINED; 0.5-MM BACKLIT SEPARATED GLUMES NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 05 · HOOD AND SHORT AWNS
tiles.details: In authentic USDA/Go Botany exact-species photographed spikelets (panel 2), rounded upper shapes resemble a hood, but these WHOLE units have not been dissected to reveal the actual upper STERILE lemma free margin. The lower fertile lemma is reportedly 1.5–2 mm with short awn about 0.3–1.5 mm; the upper reduced lemma is about 1–1.5 mm, swollen and rounded, with absent/short awn. The new arrow identifies only an upper rounded PROFILE, not a separately certified hood. A mature isolated same-voucher sterile lemma in TWO views beside 0.5-mm ruler remains essential.
tiles.short: Upper sterile lemma is a rounded 1–1.5 mm hood
tiles.status: REAL ROUNDED PROFILE ONLY; STERILE HOOD FREE MARGIN / TRUE SHORT AWN INSERTION UNPROVEN

tiles.heading: 06 · WINDMILL LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Panels 7 and 8 are DIFFERENT taxa: tumble windmillgrass Chloris verticillata with longer tiered racemes/awns and feather fingergrass C. virgata with longer fertile-lemma hairs. Panel 6 is genuine live C. cucullata habit but not excavated. Hybrids C. × subdolichostachya may be intermediate; retain scientific hold until measured mature spikelets distinguish parentage. For true species closure, compare detached sterile hoods, both glumes and short fertile-lemma awns rather than head color. New source-vouchered Austin target raceme close-up (panel 9) teaches true gross spikelet arrangement, not the measured sterile-lemma hood needed to separate parent species from hybrids. Do not label mixed parents or hybrids by heads alone.
tiles.short: Check mature florets, not only the head
tiles.status: COMPARISON PANELS AVAILABLE; SAME-SCALE DISSECTIONS NEEDED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Start with short, crowded racemes clustered into a tight windmill head. The decisive character is on a MATURE SPIKELET: the upper sterile lemma is rounded, swollen, hoodlike and about 1–1.5 mm; fertile and sterile awns are very short. A crowded head is a clue, not visual proof of the microscopic hood.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Perennial caespitose or tufted windmillgrass; Texas A&M notes occasional SHORT STOLONS, while an NRCS field account allows occasional short RHIZOMES. Whether any individual has connected runners must be proved by an actual rooted specimen, not assumed absent from a bunchgrass silhouette.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Use genuine target plants in panels 6 (Uvalde roadside), 11 (Austin narrow upright basal foliage), and 10 (Cotulla true slender attached flowering stem). These show growing tuft context, but the underground connected fibrous roots and any runners are HIDDEN, and nearby grasses in mixed vegetation may be other species. Texas A&M says short stolons sometimes occur, whereas NRCS also mentions short rhizomes; neither can be inferred here. The true ciliate MEMBRANOUS ligule is an INSIDE blade/sheath junction structure; no current photo opens it face-on beside a ruler. Do not mark an outer sheath edge, stem node or leaf hairs as that free membrane.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Fertile lemma ~1.5–2 mm with very short awn ~0.3–1.5 mm; sterile upper lemma swollen/hooded ~1–1.5 mm, awn absent or ≤1.5 mm.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Hooded windmillgrass generally has crowded shorter racemes (~2–5 cm) and a conspicuous rounded sterile hood with short awns. Tumble windmillgrass typically has longer (~5–15 cm) racemes in separated tiers and longer awns. Feather fingergrass commonly has a feathery terminal fan with long apical fertile-lemma hairs. The hybrid may be intermediate.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 1 · Source-labelled windmill racemes — separate dense head not diagnostic
panels.caption: The right-hand flowering head has radiating, one-sided spikelet-bearing racemes meeting at a visible branch junction. The dense plume on the LEFT arises from a visibly separate culm; this photograph does not prove it belongs to the same plant or demonstrates the short crowded C. cucullata racemes. Do NOT use that left plume as a hooded-windmillgrass diagnostic. Neither head resolves the microscopic sterile-lemma hood.
panels.creator: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: TEXAS LIVING HABIT — authentic flowering bunches at roadside (roots hidden)
panels.caption: Several growing hooded windmillgrass bunches are visible from leafy ground-level tufts to their actual terminal flowering heads. The image DOES NOT expose fibrous roots or prove whether any short stolons or rhizomes connect individual plants. The original photographer's public-domain JPEG is now stored with this species in GitHub, with attribution and source permissions retained.
panels.creator: Jim Conrad
panels.modifications: Re-encoded RGB JPEG; metadata/EXIF/GPS stripped; no added anatomical arrows

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE / PARENT: Chloris verticillata
panels.caption: OTHER species: authenticated locally archived tumble windmillgrass shows its long radiating racemes. The prior Joey Santore CC BY-NC media record is preserved in its source card, but is no longer this public comparison panel. Head habit alone cannot establish parentage or hybrid identity.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE — feather fingergrass actual spikelet rows (NOT hooded windmillgrass)
panels.caption: Harry Rose's CC BY 2.0 macro shows authentic Chloris virgata spikelets along one side of a flowering branch. The tightly overlapping spikelet rows alone are shared across windmillgrasses; the decisive difference is the mature fertile lemma with its long apical hair crown in C. virgata versus the reduced rounded upper sterile lemma in C. cucullata, both requiring isolated macro proof.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: AUSTIN RACEME UNDERSIDES — dense single-sided spikelet rows in hand
panels.caption: A living source-determined Austin Chloris cucullata inflorescence viewed against fingers. Each slender raceme has many tiny spikelets lined up along one side, with several short branches spreading from the same hub. The specimen confirms actual whorl architecture in another Texas locality. Neither the individual inflated sterile lemma nor its free hood margin or short awn insertion is dissected; fingers are not a true millimeter scale.
panels.creator: Tyler Cannon
panels.modifications: Original converted and metadata stripped as JPEG, no new anatomy arrows
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COTULLA ATTACHED FLOWERING CULM — terminal whorl and narrow stem
panels.caption: Cody Stricker photographed an attached hooded-windmillgrass flowering culm against red Texas soil near Cotulla. The green slender stem supports the short, tightly grouped terminal branches, with green spikelets arrayed along them. The stem remains held by the fingers; no entire root crown, measured ligule or individually isolated sterile hood is visible.
panels.creator: Cody Stricker
panels.modifications: Original converted and metadata stripped as JPEG, no new anatomy arrows
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: AUSTIN LIVING BASAL TUFT — real erect green blades at soil surface
panels.caption: A real Austin source-identified hooded windmillgrass clump shows numerous thin, upright, bluish-green leaves emerging toward the ground. Adjacent unrelated grass shoots may be present in this mixed stand, so do not label them all one plant. NO separated connected underground perennial crown, root system, rhizome, stolon node or measured inner 0.7–1 mm ciliate ligule can be demonstrated from these pixels.
